lamina propria mucosae: Contains a rich network of blood vessels
Presence of immune cells such as lymphocytes and plasma cells
May have glandular structures depending on the organ
Appears less dense than the muscularis mucosae
Stains lighter than the epithelial layer in H&E staining
May contain lymphoid aggregates or follicles
Presence of capillaries and small lymphatics
muscularis mucosae: Thin layer of smooth muscle cells.
Located between the lamina propria and the submucosa.
Appears as a continuous or slightly wavy line in cross-section.
Smooth muscle fibers are elongated and spindle-shaped.
Fibers are arranged in a parallel fashion.
May appear as a darker pink band compared to surrounding connective tissue.
In longitudinal sections, fibers may appear as long, wavy lines.
In cross-sections, fibers may appear as small, round to oval profiles.
Typically thinner than the muscularis propria.
May have a slightly undulating appearance due to contraction.
Located just beneath the glandular epithelium in the mucosa.
muscularis propria: Smooth muscle fibers arranged in bundles or layers
Nuclei are centrally located within the cells
Relatively uniform cell size and shape
Lack of striations, distinguishing it from skeletal muscle
Compact and dense appearance compared to submucosa

regression tissue: Presence of dense fibrous stroma, often appearing as a pink, collagen-rich matrix.
Scattered inflammatory cells, including lymphocytes and macrophages, within the fibrous stroma.
Reduced cellularity compared to surrounding non-regressed tissue.
Presence of hemosiderin-laden macrophages, indicating previous hemorrhage and subsequent iron deposition.
Vascular changes, such as thickened or hyalinized blood vessels.
Necrotic debris or ghost outlines of cells, indicating previous tissue damage and cell death.
Absence or reduction of viable tumor cells in areas of regression.
Calcification, which may appear as dark, basophilic deposits within the tissue.
Edema or myxoid changes, which can give the stroma a loose, pale appearance.
Presence of multinucleated giant cells, which can be part of the inflammatory response.
mucosa gastric: Presence of gastric pits: These are invaginations in the mucosal surface that are characteristic of gastric mucosa.
Glandular structure: The gastric mucosa contains tightly packed glands, which can be tubular or branched.
Columnar epithelial cells: The surface epithelium is composed of tall columnar cells, often with a clear cytoplasm due to mucin production.
Presence of parietal cells: These are large, eosinophilic cells with a central nucleus, responsible for acid production.
Chief cells: Located deeper in the glands, these cells have a basophilic cytoplasm and are responsible for pepsinogen production.
Lamina propria: A loose connective tissue layer that contains blood vessels, lymphatics, and immune cells, supporting the gastric glands.
Muscularis mucosae: A thin layer of smooth muscle that separates the mucosa from the submucosa.
Presence of mucus: The surface epithelium and neck of the glands often contain mucus, which can appear as a pale or clear area in the cytoplasm.
Basement membrane: A thin, dense layer that separates the epithelial cells from the underlying lamina propria.
Absence of villi: Unlike intestinal mucosa, gastric mucosa does not have villi.
mucosa oesophagus: Stratified squamous epithelium: The mucosa of the esophagus is lined by a non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, which appears as multiple layers of flat cells.
Basal cell layer: The basal layer of the epithelium is composed of cuboidal to columnar cells that are more basophilic (darker staining) than the superficial layers.
Lamina propria: Beneath the epithelium, the lamina propria is a layer of loose connective tissue that contains blood vessels, lymphatics, and immune cells.
Muscularis mucosae: This is a thin layer of smooth muscle fibers located beneath the lamina propria, marking the boundary between the mucosa and submucosa.
Absence of keratinization: Unlike the skin, the esophageal mucosa lacks a keratinized layer, which is important for distinguishing it from other stratified squamous epithelia.
Papillae: The interface between the epithelium and lamina propria may show papillae, which are projections of the lamina propria into the epithelium.
No glands in the mucosa: The esophageal mucosa typically lacks glands, which helps differentiate it from other parts of the gastrointestinal tract like the stomach or intestines.
Presence of lymphoid aggregates: Occasionally, small lymphoid aggregates can be found in the lamina propria, indicating immune activity.
submucosa: Presence of immune cells (e.g., lymphocytes, plasma cells)
submucosal glands: Lobular arrangement: Submucosal glands are often organized into lobules, which are clusters of glandular tissue separated by connective tissue septa.
Ductal structures: Look for ducts that connect the glands to the surface epithelium, often appearing as tubular structures lined by cuboidal or columnar epithelium.
Acinar cells: These are the secretory units of the glands, typically appearing as round or oval clusters of cells with a central lumen.
Mucous or serous cells: Depending on the type of gland, the cells may be mucous (pale, foamy cytoplasm) or serous (darker, granular cytoplasm).
Basal nuclei: The nuclei of glandular cells are usually located basally, near the basement membrane, and are round to oval in shape.
Stromal tissue: The glands are embedded in a stroma of connective tissue, which may contain blood vessels and nerves.
Vascular supply: Submucosal glands are often associated with a rich vascular network, visible as small blood vessels in the surrounding stroma.
Presence of myoepithelial cells: These are contractile cells that may be seen surrounding the acini, helping in the expulsion of glandular secretions.
Lumen size and shape: The lumens of the glands can vary in size and shape, often appearing round or oval in cross-section.
Cytoplasmic granules: In serous glands, the cytoplasm may contain zymogen granules, which are visible as small, eosinophilic granules.
tumour: Nuclear pleomorphism (variation in size and shape of nuclei)
Increased mitotic figures (more frequent cell division)
Desmoplasia (growth of fibrous or connective tissue)
Stromal reaction (changes in the supporting tissue)
ulceration: Hemorrhage or bleeding in the tissue
Irregular or ragged edges of the tissue
Presence of bacterial colonies or other pathogens
